items.title: Four Times as Old
items.question: A father is four times as old as his son. In twenty years he will be only twice as old. How old is the son now?
items.correctExplanation: Right. With the son at ten and the father at forty, twenty years gives sixty against thirty — exactly twice.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 10. Writing the father as four times the son and adding twenty years to both yields ten. Check it: forty plus twenty is sixty, and ten plus twenty is thirty.
items.lessonContent:
Age puzzles reward writing the relationship as algebra.
Add the same number of years to both people.
Substitute the relationship into the future equation.
Verify the answer by rebuilding both ages.
Share this: solve tonight one age puzzle by checking the future relationship.

items.title: Three Times Today
items.question: A mother is three times her daughter's age. In twelve years she will be twice as old. How old is the daughter now?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly. A twelve-year-old daughter and a thirty-six-year-old mother become twenty-four and forty-eight in twelve years.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 12. The trick is that the gap stays constant while the ratio shrinks; equality of the fixed gap is what nails the current ages. Twelve and thirty-six satisfy both conditions exactly.
items.lessonContent:
Ratios between ages change as years pass.
Age differences stay fixed forever.
Use the fixed gap to compare two ratio statements.
Checking the future pair confirms the algebra.
Share this: notice tonight how a fixed age gap feels smaller as ratios shift.

items.title: Sum of Fifty
items.question: A father and son's ages add to fifty, and the father is four times the son. How old is the son?
items.correctExplanation: Right. Five equal shares of fifty make ten for the son and forty for the father.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 10. If the father is four parts and the son one part, the total is five parts of fifty. Dividing gives each part, and the check confirms forty is four times ten.
items.lessonContent:
Sum-plus-ratio puzzles divide a total into parts.
Name the parts before assigning ages.
One part carries the whole answer.
Verify by rebuilding the total and ratio.
Share this: split one family total into ratio parts aloud tonight.

items.title: Thirty Years Apart
items.question: A man is thirty years older than his son. In ten years he will be three times as old. How old is the son now?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly. Five and thirty-five become fifteen and forty-five, and forty-five is three times fifteen.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 5. The fixed thirty-year gap must equal twice the son's future age, since triple minus single leaves two parts. Halving thirty gives fifteen, then subtracting the ten future years returns five.
items.lessonContent:
Fixed gaps set the scale for future ratios.
Translate the ratio into how many extra parts the gap fills.
Work backward from the future to the present.
Confirm with both ages after the wait.
Share this: use the gap method tonight on any two-age puzzle.

items.title: Ten Years Back
items.question: Ten years ago a father was seven times his son's age; now he is exactly three times. How old is the son now?
items.correctExplanation: Right. A fifteen-year-old with a forty-five-year-old father matches both the triple now and the sevenfold a decade ago.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 15. Set the father as three times the son, then apply the ten-year subtraction to both and require the older ratio. Substituting and solving gives fifteen.
items.lessonContent:
Past conditions require subtracting years from both people.
Two statements about different times pin one answer.
Solve the future or present first, then test the past.
Every condition must hold simultaneously.
Share this: test both time points tonight before trusting an age answer.

items.title: Four Times Before
items.question: Two sisters' ages sum to forty. Five years ago the elder was four times the younger. How old is the younger sister now?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly. At eleven and twenty-nine, five years earlier gave six and twenty-four — a clean fourfold.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 11. Five years ago both ages drop by five, and the total thirty divides into parts of one and four. Restoring the five years returns eleven and twenty-nine.
items.lessonContent:
Shift both ages together when moving through time.
The sum also shifts by twice the year difference.
Divide the shifted total into ratio parts.
Add the years back to report current ages.
Share this: try the shift-and-divide trick tonight on a sibling puzzle.

items.title: Reversed Ages
items.question: A mother's age and her daughter's are both two-digit numbers that are reverses of each other. Their digits sum to twelve and the ages differ by thirty-six. How old is the mother?
items.correctExplanation: Right. The digits eight and four sum to twelve and differ by four, which doubles into a thirty-six-year gap when positions swap.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 84. Reversing digits moves four times the digit difference into the age gap, so a thirty-six-year gap needs digits four apart. With a sum of twelve, the digits are eight and four, making the older age eighty-four.
items.lessonContent:
Reversed-digit puzzles convert gaps into digit differences.
A one-position swap multiplies digit gaps by nine.
Two constraints pin two unknown digits.
Test candidates by rebuilding both numbers.
Share this: construct one reverse-digit age pair tonight for a friend.

items.title: Old Ratios Fade
items.question: Five years ago, A was twice B's age. Now A is one and a half times B's age. How old is B now?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly. B at ten and A at fifteen fit the current ratio and, five years earlier, three-to-six fell to exactly double.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 10. Both descriptions must hold at once, so substitute one ratio into the other and solve. Ten and fifteen satisfy today and, five years back, six against three.
items.lessonContent:
Multiple ratio statements must all hold together.
Substitution turns prose conditions into one equation.
Non-integer ratios are easiest handled as fractions.
Checking every stated time builds confidence.
Share this: express one pair of ages as both a ratio and a difference tonight.

items.title: Three Generations Sum
items.question: A grandfather, father, and son have ages totalling one hundred and five. The father is twice the son and the grandfather is twice the father. How old is the son?
items.correctExplanation: Right. One part fifteen, two parts thirty, four parts sixty — seven equal portions of one hundred and five.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 15. The ratios make one, two, and four parts, or seven parts in total. Dividing the total by seven gives fifteen, and the chain of doublings confirms it.
items.lessonContent:
Chain ratios create power-of-two parts.
Total divided by the part count yields each share.
Rebuild every age to verify the chain.
Multi-generation puzzles are ratio puzzles in costume.
Share this: express one three-generation family as a chain of ratios tonight.

items.title: Fortieth Birthday
items.question: Today is a father's fortieth birthday and his daughter's tenth. In how many years will he be exactly twice her age?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly. Twenty years later he is sixty and she is thirty — the doubling point.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 20. The thirty-year gap must equal her future age for him to be double, so she must reach thirty. From ten, that takes twenty years.
items.lessonContent:
Doubling occurs when the gap equals the younger age.
Identify the condition before setting up algebra.
Solve for the younger age, then convert to years.
Interpret the result as elapsed time, not a date.
Share this: find tonight when a parent-child pair hits a doubling point.

items.title: Four Times Soon
items.question: A mother is thirty-five and her child is five. In how many years will she be exactly four times as old as the child?
items.correctExplanation: Right. Five years later she is forty and the child ten, a clean fourfold.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 5. Setting the future ages equal to a four-to-one ratio solves directly. Skipping the setup and guessing fails because the ratio falls as time passes.
items.lessonContent:
Ratios drift downward over time for older pairs.
Set future ages equal to the stated ratio.
Solve for elapsed years, not for ages.
Confirm by rebuilding the future pair.
Share this: track tonight how a fixed ratio loosens with every passing year.

items.title: Six Years Ago
items.question: Two friends' ages sum to thirty. Six years ago one was twice the other. How old is the older friend now?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly. Eighteen and twelve sum to thirty, and six years earlier those were twelve and six.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 18. Six years ago the total was eighteen, split one-to-two into six and twelve. Adding six years back gives twelve and eighteen.
items.lessonContent:
Shift the total before splitting by ratio.
The total drops by twice the elapsed years.
Ratio parts then give each past age.
Restore the years to report the present.
Share this: solve one past-ratio puzzle tonight using the shifted total.

items.title: Five Times Before
items.question: A man is three times as old as his brother. Six years ago he was five times as old. How old is the younger brother now?
items.correctExplanation: Right. Twelve and thirty-six become six and thirty when six years are removed — a fivefold gap.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 12. Substituting the triple relationship into the earlier fivefold condition and solving gives the younger age. Both conditions then check out.
items.lessonContent:
Older ratios appear further back in time.
Combine a present ratio with a past one by substitution.
Solve for the younger age first.
Rebuild the past pair to verify.
Share this: chart tonight how sibling ratios change from past to present.

items.title: As Old as Now
items.question: A man is forty-two and his son is twelve. When the son becomes as old as his father is today, how old will the father be?
items.correctExplanation: Right. The son needs thirty years to reach forty-two, and the father gains those same thirty years, landing at seventy-two.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 72. The son gains thirty years to match today's father, and time adds to both equally. Reaching a fixed age is simple addition once the wait is measured.
items.lessonContent:
Fixed-age conditions make elapsed time the unknown.
Measure the wait first, then apply it to everyone.
Both ages advance by the same number of years.
Reference points like today's age anchor the math.
Share this: figure out tonight when your age will match an earlier target.

items.title: Twins and Father
items.question: A father and his twin sons have ages summing to sixty. The father is exactly twice the age of one son. How old is the father?
items.correctExplanation: Right. Two sons at fifteen each plus a thirty-year-old father make sixty.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 30. The twins count as two parts and the father as two parts, so the total splits into four equal shares of fifteen. The father takes two shares, thirty.
items.lessonContent:
Twins create duplicated parts in ratio puzzles.
Count every person as a share of the total.
Divide, then reconstruct the family.
Identical ages double one unknown, not two.
Share this: split one family total into shares tonight as a party trick.

items.title: Memory Arithmetic
items.question: In eight years a girl will be three times as old as she was four years ago. How old is she now?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly. Ten plus eight is eighteen, and ten minus four is six, which is one third of eighteen.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 10. Future and past conditions both reference her current age, so both translate directly into one equation. Solving gives ten, and both ages verify.
items.lessonContent:
Conditions can point backward and forward simultaneously.
Translate each into the same unknown.
Solving both together beats guessing ages.
Verify using both time directions.
Share this: write one past-and-future condition tonight for your own age.

items.title: Married Twenty Years
items.question: A couple has been married for twenty years, and the husband was twenty-five on their wedding day. How old is he now?
items.correctExplanation: Right. Twenty-five plus twenty years of marriage gives forty-five.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 45. The wedding age anchors the arithmetic, and the years since simply add on. Anniversary puzzles are ordinary addition wearing a story hat.
items.lessonContent:
Anchors plus elapsed time solve timeline questions.
Identify the reference event's dated value.
Add the interval in the correct direction.
Stories dress up simple addition; find the anchor.
Share this: compute one family anniversary age tonight without a calculator.

items.title: Three Under Twice
items.question: My age is three years less than twice my sister's, and together we are twenty-seven. How old is my sister?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly. A ten-year-old sister and a seventeen-year-old me add to twenty-seven, and seventeen is three less than twenty.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 10. Replace my age with the described expression and solve the single equation. Checking both conditions confirms ten.
items.lessonContent:
Translate descriptive phrases into expressions.
Replace one unknown to reduce to a single variable.
Check that every clause holds.
Descriptive arithmetic is just algebra in words.
Share this: encode one family age rule as an expression tonight.

items.title: Sum of Siblings
items.question: A father's age equals the sum of his three children's ages, which are five, seven, and ten. How old is the father?
items.correctExplanation: Right. Five plus seven plus ten equals twenty-two, the father's age.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 22. The stated relationship is an equality, so simple addition of the children's ages finishes the job. Overcomplicating this one is the only real trap.
items.lessonContent:
Some puzzles are one-step addition in disguise.
Read the relationship before assumed complexity.
Sum the given parts exactly.
Simple answers deserve the same checking.
Share this: note tonight how often a 'hard' problem is plain arithmetic.

items.title: A Decade Either Way
items.question: Ten years from now a man will be three times as old as he was ten years ago. How old is he now?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly. Twenty plus ten is thirty, and twenty minus ten is ten — a clean triple.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 20. Both conditions describe the same current age, so one equation settles it. Thirty against ten verifies the result immediately.
items.lessonContent:
Symmetric past and future conditions are one equation.
Both sides reference the same present unknown.
Solve, then verify in both directions.
Symmetry often hides in plain phrasing.
Share this: find one symmetric condition in a timeline puzzle tonight.

items.title: Five Years Senior
items.question: A woman is five years older than her husband, and their ages total seventy-five. How old is the woman?
items.correctExplanation: Right. A thirty-five-year-old husband and a forty-year-old wife total seventy-five.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 40. Subtract the five-year head start from the total, halve it for the husband, then add the difference back for the wife. The check confirms both clauses.
items.lessonContent:
Remove the known difference, then split evenly.
Add the difference back to the older party.
Verification catches sign errors quickly.
Word problems hide clean arithmetic under names.
Share this: solve one difference-plus-total puzzle tonight mentally.

items.title: Twice the Young Man
items.question: A father is fifty and his son is fourteen. In how many years will the father be exactly twice as old as his son?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly. Twenty-two years later the father is seventy-two and the son thirty-six.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 22. The thirty-six-year gap must equal the son's future age for doubling. From fourteen, reaching thirty-six takes twenty-two years.
items.lessonContent:
Doubling happens when the gap equals the younger age.
Work from the gap rather than ratio guessing.
Convert the needed future age into elapsed years.
Historic doubling puzzles all use this shortcut.
Share this: explain tonight why the gap determines any doubling date.

items.title: Born at Twenty-Two
items.question: A mother and daughter's ages sum to forty-four, and the mother was twenty-two when the daughter was born. How old is the daughter?
items.correctExplanation: Right. An eleven-year-old daughter with a thirty-three-year-old mother totals forty-four and matches the birth-age clue.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 11. The mother's age at the birth is exactly their fixed gap, so subtract that gap from the total and halve for the daughter. The check confirms the birth age.
items.lessonContent:
Birth ages encode the fixed gap between parent and child.
Gap plus total determines both ages.
Subtract the gap, halve the remainder.
Real family data often embeds the gap directly.
Share this: derive one friend's parent age from the birth-date clue.

items.title: Two Years Apart
items.question: Three siblings are each two years apart in age, and their ages sum to twenty-four. How old is the youngest?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly. Six, eight, and ten are two years apart and total twenty-four.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 6. Three equal ages would total twenty-four as eight each; spread the extra four years across the spacing to get six, eight, and ten. Averaging is the shortcut.
items.lessonContent:
Evenly spaced ages average to the middle value.
Divide the total by the count for the center.
Step down for younger, up for older.
Spacing puzzles are averaging puzzles.
Share this: average one set of spaced ages tonight in your head.

items.title: Product of Ages
items.question: A brother is twice as old as his sister, and the product of their ages is seventy-two. How old is the sister?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly. If the sister is six, the brother is twelve, and six times twelve is seventy-two.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 6. Writing the brother as double the sister turns the product into twice her squared age. Seventy-two halved is thirty-six, whose square root is six.
items.lessonContent:
Products of ages need one variable expressed in another.
Doubling relationships turn products into squares.
Factoring or square roots finish the job.
Test a candidate to verify the product.
Share this: turn one product-of-ages puzzle tonight into a square.
